Onion Export

Red Onion Exporter from Maharashtra: A Buyer's Guide to Sourcing from India

A practical guide for international buyers covering Maharashtra's onion supply, exporter verification, red onion specifications, grading, packing, quotations, documentation and shipment planning.

September 2026 · 10 min read

Why Maharashtra matters to international red onion buyers

Maharashtra is the leading onion-producing state in India. APEDA reports that Maharashtra accounted for 44.07% of India's onion production in 2024–25. APEDA also describes two major onion crop cycles in India, with harvesting broadly beginning from November to January and again from January to May.

For a buyer, however, a large production base does not automatically mean that every exporter can supply the required grade. The useful question is whether the exporter can consistently match your required red onion variety, size, quality, packing, quantity, shipment window and destination requirements.

Buyer principle: Do not select a Maharashtra onion exporter only because the quotation is low. Compare the product specification, quality tolerance, packing, documentation, shipment plan and total delivered cost on the same basis.

1. Understand what you are actually buying

“Red onion” is not a complete export specification. Before contacting exporters, prepare a written buying specification so every supplier quotes against the same requirements.

  • Product: fresh red onions for export.
  • Size: define the required diameter range and acceptable tolerance.
  • Quality: specify acceptable limits for decay, cuts, bruises, sprouting, immature bulbs and other defects.
  • Appearance: specify skin condition, colour, dryness and overall uniformity expected at loading.
  • Quantity: state tonnes, bags or container requirement and whether the figure is net cargo weight.
  • Packing: specify bag type, net weight per bag, markings and palletisation if required.
  • Destination: give the destination country and discharge port.
  • Delivery term: clearly state whether you want FOB, CFR or CIF and name the port.
  • Shipment window: give a realistic loading period rather than only saying “urgent”.

2. Why Maharashtra is important in the Indian onion supply chain

APEDA identifies Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha among India's major onion-producing states, with Maharashtra ranking first in 2024–25.

For red onion buyers, Maharashtra can therefore be an important sourcing base, but the exact procurement point still matters. An exporter may source from different agricultural markets, aggregators, packhouses or farmers depending on the season and specification. Ask where the onions are being procured, where they are graded and where the export packing is performed.

3. What to verify before choosing an exporter

A serious buyer should verify the supplier rather than relying only on photographs, WhatsApp messages or a website. APEDA maintains an Exporter's Directory that can be used as one source for checking registered exporters and their declared product categories.

Exporter checkWhat the buyer should ask for
Business identityLegal business name, registered address, contact details and export-related registration information.
Product capabilityRed onion type, size range, available quantity and quality specification.
SourcingCurrent sourcing market/region, procurement method and season availability.
GradingHow onions are sorted, sized and rejected before packing.
PackingActual bag type, net weight, bag dimensions, markings and loading configuration.
Quality controlInspection process, defect tolerance and how shipment quality is documented.
LogisticsLoading location, export gateway, expected transit plan and vessel schedule.
DocumentationAbility to provide commercial and shipment documents required by the buyer and destination.

4. Red onion size and grading: make the specification measurable

Size is one of the first points that can create disputes between buyer and seller. A buyer should not simply write “big red onion”. Give a defined size range and agree how size will be measured and tolerated.

Typical points to define in the purchase specification

  • Minimum and maximum bulb diameter.
  • Allowed percentage outside the agreed size range, if any.
  • Maximum percentage of damaged, rotten or sprouted bulbs.
  • Skin and neck condition expected at shipment.
  • Whether mixed sizes are permitted.
  • Whether quality is assessed at the packhouse, loading point or through a third-party inspection.

Do not assume that a supplier's internal grade name means the same thing as your import-market specification. Put the measurable requirement in the proforma invoice or purchase order.

5. Inspect quality before a large shipment

Onions are an agricultural product, so visual appearance can change between procurement, packing and arrival. For a new exporter, consider a representative sample, inspection report, quality sheet or pre-shipment inspection arrangement suitable for the transaction.

Important quality checks

  • Firmness: bulbs should be appropriately firm for the agreed specification.
  • Dryness: outer skin and neck should be suitable for export handling and the agreed destination requirements.
  • Damage: check for cuts, bruises and mechanical injury.
  • Decay: reject affected bulbs and define an acceptable tolerance.
  • Sprouting: check for visible sprouting according to the agreed grade.
  • Uniformity: inspect whether the actual load matches the agreed size range.
  • Pack weight: verify net weight against the contract specification.

APEDA notes that modern packhouses are available in production zones for sorting, grading and packing, and that guidelines exist for maximum residue levels and quality parameters.

6. Ask for a quotation that can actually be compared

A price such as “USD 300 per ton” is incomplete unless you know what it includes. APEDA's export guidance says an export enquiry should specify product size, quantity, delivery schedule, price basis such as FOB or C&F/CIF, dispatch mode, packing, payment terms, inspection requirements and certificate-of-origin requirements.

For each quotation, ask the exporter to state:

  • Price per metric ton.
  • Currency.
  • Incoterm and named place/port.
  • Net weight per bag and total net shipment weight.
  • Packaging cost, if separate.
  • Inspection or certification charges, if applicable.
  • Estimated loading date.
  • Payment terms.
  • Validity of the quotation.
  • Any charges excluded from the quoted price.

7. FOB, CFR and CIF can change the real buying cost

Two exporters can quote different prices and still have similar economics once freight and other buyer-side costs are included. Compare quotations on the same Incoterms® basis and the same destination.

Price basisWhat the buyer should clarify
FOBConfirm the named port and understand which costs are included up to the agreed delivery point.
CFRConfirm the destination port and the ocean freight included in the quotation; clarify insurance responsibility separately.
CIFConfirm the destination port, included freight and insurance terms, and the coverage actually provided.

The commercial comparison should ultimately focus on the buyer's expected landed cost, not only the supplier's headline onion price.

8. Understand the export documentation

APEDA lists commonly used export documents such as the commercial invoice, bill of lading, certificate of origin, inspection certification where required, insurance certificate where applicable and export packing list. The exact document set depends on the transaction and the importing country's requirements.

Before confirming an order, agree who is responsible for preparing each document and whether your destination requires additional certificates, inspection or product-specific compliance documents.

9. Check the current onion export policy before every shipment

Onion export policy has changed through government notifications in recent years. For example, DGFT Notification No. 10/2024-25 changed the policy for the specified onion tariff item from prohibited to free subject to a Minimum Export Price of USD 550 per metric ton at that time.

That historical notification should not be treated as a permanent current rule. Exporters and buyers should verify the latest DGFT/APEDA notification and applicable conditions immediately before shipment. APEDA maintains a current notifications page that includes onion-related DGFT notifications.

10. Plan the shipment from farm or packhouse to port

For fresh onions, logistics planning should connect procurement, grading, packing, inland transport, port cut-off and vessel schedule. Ask the exporter where the cargo will be packed, how long it will remain before loading, which export gateway is planned and how the shipment schedule will be managed.

A low factory or packhouse price can become less attractive if inland transport, port charges, delays or additional handling materially increase the final cost. Request the complete commercial and logistics assumptions before comparing offers.

11. Use a buyer checklist before placing the order

Before confirming a Maharashtra red onion shipment, verify:

  • Supplier identity and export credentials checked.
  • Red onion specification written and accepted by both sides.
  • Size range and quality tolerance clearly defined.
  • Sample or inspection process agreed where appropriate.
  • Packing and net weight confirmed.
  • Total quantity and shipment window confirmed.
  • FOB/CFR/CIF basis and named port confirmed.
  • Payment terms documented.
  • Required certificates and destination compliance checked.
  • Current onion export policy verified before shipment.
  • Final documents and shipping responsibilities assigned.

Final takeaway

For an international buyer, sourcing red onions from Maharashtra is best approached as a documented supply-chain process: define the product → verify the exporter → agree measurable quality → inspect the shipment → compare commercial terms → confirm documentation → plan logistics → verify current export requirements.

Maharashtra's large share of India's onion production makes it an important sourcing base, but the exporter's ability to deliver the exact specification consistently is what should drive the commercial evaluation. APEDA's current onion information and exporter directory can provide useful starting points for market and supplier checks.
